article.overview: A lunar polar volatile analyser is a scientific instrument that identifies the gases (volatiles) released from lunar soil, or from samples of it, in permanently shadowed or cold polar regions. Its main purpose is to determine whether the regolith contains water or other volatile compounds and, where possible, their chemical and isotopic signatures. The clearest published example in the sources reviewed is the Mass Spectrometer Observing Lunar Operations (MSolo), a mass spectrometer that NASA developed for the Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER) [1][2]. MSolo was later carried on the Intuitive Machines IM-2 mission (PRIME-1), which landed at Mons Mouton on 6 March 2025 but came to rest on its side. NASA reports that the PRIME-1 instruments could not complete their science goals [4]. The instrument therefore has a partly verified flight history, but no verified volatile science data are reported here [4][5].
article.description:
"Lunar polar volatile analyser" is a generic class name in the catalogue, not a single standard design. In general, such an instrument includes a gas-sampling or heating interface that releases volatiles from soil or drill cuttings, a sensor that identifies the released gas species, and electronics that record the results with time and location information. The volatiles of interest include water and related hydrogen-bearing species, and the isotope ratios of those species can help scientists interpret their origin [1].

The MSolo example is a commercial off-the-shelf mass spectrometer that NASA modified for space use. NASA describes it as "a modified commercial off-the-shelf mass spectrometer built to withstand the harsh lunar environment" [2]. The vendor identifies the base instrument as the INFICON Transpector MPH quadrupole mass spectrometer [5]. The NASA source record states that MSolo was designed to identify low-molecular-weight volatiles between m/z 1 and 100 with unit mass resolution, including D/H and O18/O16 bearing species [1].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The stated purpose of MSolo is to detect and measure volatiles along the VIPER traverse and near a drilling site, with the goal of producing lunar water resource maps [1]. The sources describe two sampling situations: gases that might be released as the rover wheels disturb the soil while driving, and gases released from drill cuttings brought to the surface. In the planned VIPER operations, the drill was to reach about one metre, and the released gases would be analysed at the surface [1][3]. The NASA PRIME-1 page describes the same measurement role on the IM-2 lander: MSOLO was to examine TRIDENT drill samples for subsurface volatiles [4].

Applications for a lunar polar volatile analyser therefore include mapping water distribution, testing whether water is accessible within the regolith, and supplying chemical and isotopic data that complement drilling, neutron and remote-sensing observations. These applications remain proposed objectives drawn from the cited sources; no verified water result from MSolo is reported here.
article.operating_principle:
The vendor describes MSolo's base instrument as a quadrupole mass spectrometer [5]. In general terms, a mass spectrometer ionises gas molecules and separates the resulting ions by their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z); a quadrupole instrument does this by applying oscillating electric fields to four rods, and the detector records the abundance of each selected mass. For MSolo, the reported mass range is m/z 1 to 100 with unit mass resolution [1]. Unit mass resolution means that ions differing by one mass unit can be distinguished, which is sufficient for many low-molecular-weight species but not for resolving all ambiguous mass overlaps. The sources reviewed do not describe the MSolo-specific inlet, ion source or control electronics, so those details are not asserted here.

For a surface volatile analyser, the key engineering problem is that the instrument must receive a representative sample of released gas. Gas from undisturbed soil is generally very difficult to measure, so the interface design (how soil is disturbed, heated or sealed, and how gas is transferred to the sensor) strongly affects the interpretation of results [1].
article.scientific_importance:
Water in lunar polar regions matters for both science and future exploration. Scientists need to determine where water occurs, in what form and at what concentration, and whether its isotopic composition indicates its source. Direct measurements of released gases are one way to address these questions. The MSolo instrument was designed to make such measurements at a planned polar site and to link them with drilling and traverse data [1][3].

The importance of this class of instrument depends on verified measurements. The NASA PRIME-1 page reports that the mission did not achieve its goals [4]. The vendor reports that MSolo operated during transit and on the surface for a few hours, and that it collected 136 full spectra [5]. Neither NASA nor a peer-reviewed publication in the sources reviewed confirms those vendor figures, so no volatile composition or water finding from the flight is reported in this article.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a lunar polar volatile analyser. Instruments in this class may differ substantially in sensor type, sampling interface, thermal control, power, data handling and mass. The example below is the only instrument in this class described in detail in the sources reviewed. Values that the sources do not publish are marked as not publicly specified.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A polar surface volatile analyser must operate in a vacuum, with extreme temperature variation, radiation and dust exposure. It must also survive launch and landing loads and handle a sample interface that can be contaminated by the regolith. The MSolo source describes ruggedisation for the lunar environment [2], but the environmental qualification levels (temperature, vibration, radiation) are not publicly specified in the sources read. The PRIME-1 landing illustrates the operational importance of landing attitude: NASA states that the lander was on its side, so the instruments could not complete their work [4]. Power, thermal control, data handling and the sample-handling interface are likewise not publicly specified for MSolo in these sources.
article.limitations: The main limitations are measurement-related. A mass spectrometer reports the species it detects, but it cannot by itself show where those species were held in the soil or how the sampling process altered them. Unit mass resolution cannot separate every overlapping mass peak. Data from a rover traverse depend on the location, the disturbance mechanism and the sampling interface. Results from one site cannot be assumed to represent the whole polar region. For the IM-2 attempt, the vendor reports that the drill could not be activated [5], so the sampling path that the instrument was designed to use was not exercised as planned.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The MSolo transport history is partly verified and partly superseded by changes to the VIPER plan. The IM-2 (PRIME-1) landing is the documented flight delivery; the 2023 VIPER plan and the 2025 Blue Moon MK-1 plan are programme-level plans for the rover.
transportation_process: Earth integration: NASA reported that MSOLO arrived at Johnson Space Center on 27 February 2023 and would be integrated with the VIPER rover there [2]. The image metadata describes the instrument being unpacked and functionally tested in the High Bay of Building 9S [2]; this description comes from the image metadata and was not independently verified.
Launch and lunar transfer (2023 plan): NASA's 2023 article stated that MSOLO, as part of VIPER, would launch on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy through NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative [2].

Flown delivery: NASA's PRIME-1 page names MSOLO as a PRIME-1 instrument and reports that the IM-2 lander touched down at Mons Mouton on 6 March 2025, on its side [4]. The vendor reports that MSolo was operational during transit [5]. The NASA page does not describe MSolo's operations in detail.

Current VIPER delivery plan: A NASA Science page states that, following an announcement dated 19 September 2025, VIPER and its instruments will be delivered to Mons Mouton by a Blue Origin Blue Moon MK-1 lander as part of task order CS-7 [3]. The page does not name MSolo and does not state the launch vehicle for that delivery.

Deployment and setup: The MSolo measurements were designed to be made while the rover drives and during drilling, which implies operation on the rover rather than as a separately deployed instrument [1][3]. The PRIME-1 page describes MSOLO's intended role in examining TRIDENT drill samples [4]. Deployment mechanisms, power and data interfaces, and thermal interfaces for MSolo are not publicly specified in the sources read.

Compatibility: No compatibility with a named lander can be verified from these sources. The IM-2 landing documents MSolo's flight history, not an interface verification for other landers, and the Blue Moon MK-1 delivery is not an interface verification for MSolo.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The MSolo measurements were designed to be made while the rover drives and during drilling, so the instrument is described as operating on the rover [1][3]. The PRIME-1 page describes the instrument's intended role in examining TRIDENT drill samples [4]. Deployment mechanisms for the instrument itself are not publicly specified in the sources read.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The VIPER planning documents of 2023 describe Earth integration at Johnson Space Center and a planned Falcon Heavy and Griffin lander delivery [2]. The IM-2 (PRIME-1) mission carried MSolo to the lunar surface and landed on its side in March 2025 [4][5]. The later Blue Moon MK-1 delivery for VIPER is described by NASA [3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander can be verified from the sources read. Lander interface, mass, power, data and thermal requirements for MSolo are not publicly specified, the IM-2 flight documents MSolo's flight history rather than a verified interface for other landers, and the Blue Moon MK-1 delivery should not be treated as an interface verification.

article.historical_significance: MSolo was developed as a science instrument for VIPER, a NASA mission designed to explore lunar polar volatiles [1][2]. It was later flown on the IM-2 (PRIME-1) mission, which landed on its side in March 2025 [4]. Its historical significance therefore lies in two points: it is a documented polar volatile measurement concept [1], and its flight attempt is a documented, partly completed example of a volatile analyser on the lunar surface, with the outcome shaped by landing attitude [4][5].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- The catalogue name describes a class of instruments, not one design. MSolo is an example and should not be treated as the only or standard example.
- Mass, power, dimensions and environmental qualification values are not publicly specified in the sources read. The NTRS MSolo record [1] was reviewed as an abstract in this run, and its linked Word document could not be extracted, so the full text may contain specifications.
- Flight status: MSolo was on the IM-2 (PRIME-1) lander, which landed on its side at Mons Mouton on 6 March 2025 [4]. NASA states that the instruments did not accomplish their goals [4]. The NASA PRIME-1 page does not state whether MSOLO powered on or recorded data.
- The vendor states that MSolo operated during transit and on the surface for several hours and collected 136 full spectra [5]. These are vendor statements. They were not confirmed against a NASA or peer-reviewed source in this run, and the spectrum count should be treated as unverified.
- A NASA presentation, "PRIME-1: MSolo Overview and Results" (April 2026, NTRS 20260003150) [6], was identified in search. Its text could not be extracted in this run, so no results from it are reported. It may contain NASA-reported surface data.
- A 2025 NASA technical report on ground-test monitoring of MSolo drill cuttings was identified in search but not read. It describes pre-flight testing and is not evidence of flight performance.
- The VIPER status is inconsistent across sources. Secondary sources reported a July 2024 NASA intent to end VIPER and conflicting launch vehicles for the Blue Moon MK-1 delivery; these claims were not verified against NASA primary sources in this run. The NASA VIPER page [3] gives the Blue Moon MK-1 delivery plan and reports three instruments in its body text but four in its sidebar.
- Other lunar polar volatile analysers in the catalogue were not researched for this article.
- The NASA image was retrieved as a JPEG and its embedded metadata was read; its visual content was not independently interpreted. NASA media terms should be checked before republication.
- Lunar landing-site or location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.

data_quality_notes: Version 2 rerun. Research used 4 web searches and 8 page or document reads in this run. The v1 article is unchanged.

Flight status changed from v1. NASA's PRIME-1 page (IM-2 lander, landed 6 March 2025 on its side, science goals not achieved) confirms MSolo was on the flown lander. The vendor's statements of operation during transit and on the surface, and of 136 spectra, are not confirmed by NASA or a peer-reviewed source.

Mass, power, dimensions and environmental qualification of MSolo are not publicly specified in the sources read. The NTRS record was reviewed as an abstract; its linked Word document could not be extracted, so specifications may exist there.
The NASA PRIME-1 overview and results presentation (NTRS 20260003150) was identified in search but its PDF text could not be extracted; no results from it are reported.
A 2025 NASA technical report on ground-test monitoring of MSolo drill cuttings was identified in search but not read; it is pre-flight testing only.

The VIPER status is inconsistent across sources. Secondary sources reported a July 2024 NASA intent to end VIPER and conflicting launch vehicles for the Blue Moon MK-1 delivery; these were not verified against NASA primary sources. The NASA VIPER page gives inconsistent instrument counts (three in the body text, four in the sidebar).
The vendor article is undated in the fetched text. The INFICON 136-spectrum figure was also reported in a search summary described as AI-generated, so it is treated as unverified.
Image viper_msolo_at_jsc.jpg resolved as image/jpeg and its metadata was read, but its visual content was not independently interpreted; the description and credit rely on embedded metadata.
No compatibility claim is made for any named lander. The IM-2 and Blue Moon MK-1 missions are reported from NASA and vendor sources and do not establish interface compatibility for MSolo.
No lunar landing-site or location recommendations are included, per the user's deferral.
